task_row_model.query: In a behavioral research study training a binary classifier, what minimum per-class sample size should I aim for, what train/validation/test split is recommended, and how should class labels be preprocessed before training?

documents.content: In experimental psychology reporting, power analyses commonly recommend a minimum of about 50 observations per experimental group or class to detect medium-sized effects with conventional alpha and power thresholds. Researchers emphasize balancing class sizes where possible because asymmetry across classes can bias estimated effects and classifier performance. This recommendation builds on decades of behavioral research practices; early laboratory psychology in the late 19th century focused on small, well-controlled samples, but modern applied studies stress larger, balanced samples to improve generalizability. Adjacent terminology such as "group" and "cohort" is often used interchangeably with "class" in behavioral datasets, but the key practical point is to secure sufficient examples per class for stable estimates.

Machine-learning practitioners frequently adopt a standard train/validation/test split to assess model fit and generalization. A common default is 70% training, 15% validation, and 15% testing; this preserves a sizable training set while reserving enough holdout data for tuning and final evaluation. For small datasets some teams use 80/10/10, but 70/15/15 remains a pragmatic compromise. Importantly, splits should be done with stratified sampling for classification tasks so the proportion of classes is preserved across train, validation, and test sets. Journalistic guides and short tutorials repeat this advice as a best practice for ensuring that model selection and reported metrics reflect balanced class representation.

A practical preprocessing checklist for supervised classification emphasizes converting categorical class labels into a binary numerical format for binary tasks: map positive/negative or yes/no strings to 1 and 0 respectively. Before splitting data, remove records with missing or undefined class labels rather than attempting to infer them, because label imputation can introduce bias in supervised learning. After labels are finalized, apply any feature scaling or imputation for predictors, but label encoding must be completed first so that stratified splits preserve class proportions. Informal engineering notes also mention keeping a copy of original label mappings for interpretability during reporting.

Reference summaries on classification often include definitional boilerplate about common metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, and many entries discuss logistic regression and support vector machines as canonical algorithms. Some background pieces present unrelated case studies, for instance a large-scale marketing campaign where millions of observations made even small effect sizes significant, which is not applicable to small behavioral datasets. Other tangential commentary covers the historical evolution of evaluation metrics and speculative trends in automated model selection; these broader notes provide context but do not change the practical sampling, splitting, and preprocessing recommendations applicable to modest-sized behavioral research projects.

task_row_model.golden_answer: Aim for at least 50 observations per class and keep classes balanced where possible. Split data 70% train, 15% validation, 15% test using stratified sampling to preserve class proportions. Preprocess labels by encoding them as binary 1/0 and remove records with missing or undefined class labels before splitting.
